solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: One caught clergyman brushing ends of chapel very carefully

indicators.note: the ends of words are their final letters, so only the last letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: one is the indefinite article a
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
a curate is an assistant parish priest
the final letters of these two words

explanation.surface: A careful worshipper is caught dusting a clergyman's chapel with great care.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very' looks like it belongs with 'carefully', but its last letter is part of the wordplay; 'brushing' just means the clergyman touches what follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something accurately means doing it precisely and with close attention, which is to work with care.

clue.text: Puncture in car upsetting – it’s potentially fatal

indicators.note: upsetting means overturning, so the letters of car are knocked into a new order
in means the puncture is placed inside the other word

blocks.note: a puncture is a hole
taken as written

explanation.surface: A flat tyre on a car can lead to a deadly accident.
explanation.definitionFit: Cholera is an acute bacterial infection of the gut which can kill through severe dehydration if untreated.

clue.text: No area on BBC is free

indicators.note: no area tells us the abbreviation for area is removed from the word that follows

blocks.note: a is the abbreviation for area
Auntie, or Auntie Beeb, is the British nickname for the BBC

explanation.surface: A region with no BBC coverage gets its programmes free of charge.
explanation.walkthrough: The BBC, Britain's public broadcaster, is affectionately called Auntie.
explanation.definitionFit: To untie is to release from a knot or binding, so it serves as the verb free.

clue.text: State love about avocado pear when hollowed out and pitted

indicators.note: about means turned around and mixed, so the letters of love are rearranged
hollowed out removes all the inside letters, leaving just the two outer ones

blocks.note: AL is the postal abbreviation for Alabama
taken as written
the first and last letters of the phrase

explanation.surface: Someone declares their love for an avocado once it is hollowed out and the stone removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pitted' suggests the avocado's stone being taken out; it means having small cavities.
explanation.definitionFit: Alveolar describes tissue full of tiny sockets or cavities, like lung air sacs, so it means pitted with small hollows.

clue.text: Shout and stress a point!

blocks.note: an exclamation is a sudden cry or shout
to mark something is to emphasise or note it

explanation.surface: An instruction to raise your voice and argue forcefully.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: the punctuation that signals a shout and stresses a point, and the clue ends with one.
explanation.definitionFit: This punctuation symbol follows a shouted or emphatic sentence, marking strong feeling or added emphasis.

clue.text: Old farmer with money arranged to purchase acre

indicators.note: arranged means put into a new order, so the letters of money are reordered
to purchase is to take hold of, so the rearranged word grips the abbreviation for acre

blocks.note: taken as written
a is the abbreviation for acre

explanation.surface: A farmer of old arranged his finances so as to buy another acre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'purchase' looks like buying, but it means grip or hold.
explanation.definitionFit: A yeoman was historically an English small landowner who farmed his own land, a free farmer of former times.

clue.text: Potty not right upstairs

blocks.note: first meaning: crazy, in British slang
second meaning: an idiom for being mentally unsound, 'upstairs' meaning in the head

explanation.walkthrough: 'Potty' can suggest a child's toilet and 'upstairs' a house, but both parts describe someone who has lost their wits.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaga is informal for senile or crazy, matching both the British slang potty and the idiom about one's head.

clue.text: Looking at restraining ego in government

indicators.note: restraining means holding in, so the answer is held within the words that follow

blocks.note: drop the first letter and the last five

explanation.surface: Examining how ministers keep their vanity in check.
explanation.definitionFit: A going-over is a careful inspection, and going over something means examining or reviewing it closely.

clue.text: One more prepared to sacrifice nothing in taste?

definitions.text: One more prepared to sacrifice nothing in taste?

blocks.clueFragment: One more prepared to sacrifice nothing
blocks.note: surface reading: a person readier than most to give up everything, perhaps for a cause
setter's reading: a food lover who refuses to compromise at all on flavour

explanation.walkthrough: The first words suggest a self-sacrificing martyr; the last two turn it into someone who won't give an inch on fine food.
explanation.definitionFit: A connoisseur of good food and drink demands the best flavours and will not accept any lowering of standards.

clue.text: Top ground with English linesman?

indicators.note: something ground is crushed and broken up, so its letters are mixed into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A football linesman stands on the touchline beside some top-quality English pitch.
explanation.walkthrough: A linesman normally runs the touchline at football; here, with the question mark, it is someone who writes lines of verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A poet composes lines of verse, so the setter jokingly calls such a writer a man of lines.

clue.text: Successful joke back in base

indicators.note: going back means reading the word for joke from right to left
placed in means set inside the word for base

blocks.note: rot is nonsense, something not to be taken seriously
base in the sense of low, mean and wicked

explanation.surface: A winning prank is played again back at the team's home base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'base' looks like a place, but it is the adjective meaning morally low.
explanation.definitionFit: A victorious side has won, and winning is exactly what being successful in a contest means.

clue.text: The ore’s sifted for this object

indicators.note: ore that is sifted is sorted and shaken about, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the apostrophe-s is ignored; taken as written

explanation.surface: Miners sift the ore to separate out what they are after.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of 'ore's' is read as 'is', leaving 'sifted' as the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereto is a formal word meaning to this matter or for this purpose, as in documents attached hereto.

clue.text: Friendly when not at home

blocks.note: surface reading: someone who is warm and sociable whenever they are out of the house
setter's reading: a friendly is a non-competitive sports match, here one played at the opponent's ground

explanation.walkthrough: 'Friendly' reads as an adjective about a person, but in sport it is a noun for an exhibition match.
explanation.definitionFit: A match played at the opposing team's ground rather than on home turf, which a friendly fixture can be.

clue.text: Survey finds gold in American republic

indicators.note: in means one piece is placed inside the name of the country

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
the Central American country

explanation.surface: A geological survey discovers gold deposits in a Central American country.
explanation.definitionFit: A panorama is a wide view or comprehensive overview, and a survey can mean a broad general view of a scene or subject.

clue.text: Girl twisted toes around swing

indicators.note: twisted means bent out of shape, so the letters are put in another order
around means wrapped about the girl's name, which sits inside

blocks.note: taken as written
a girl's name, as in the singer Cilla Black

explanation.surface: A girl curls her toes as she rides on a playground swing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swing' reads as the playground seat, but here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To oscillate is to move back and forth regularly, exactly as a pendulum or a child's seat does when it swings.

clue.text: Something expressed by a cross voice

blocks.note: first meaning: a choice marked with an X on a ballot paper
second meaning: a say in a decision

explanation.walkthrough: 'a cross voice' suggests an angry tone; 'cross' is really the X on a ballot paper.
explanation.definitionFit: Voters mark ballots with an X, and having a vote means having a voice in a collective decision.

clue.text: Reform’s concerning company to a great extent

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
Co is the abbreviation for company
very means greatly or extremely

explanation.surface: A reform programme is largely about the business of a company.
explanation.definitionFit: A recovery is a return to a better or healthier state, which is what reform seeks to achieve.

clue.text: Impressive people with refined tastes? Not half!

indicators.note: not half asks for only half of the word to be kept, the rest dropped

blocks.note: epicures are connoisseurs of fine food and drink

explanation.surface: Are gourmets impressive? The British retort 'Not half!' means very much so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'absolutely', but here it means keep only the first half of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Epic is used informally to describe something grand, heroic or hugely impressive in scale.

clue.text: Assume priest has awful temper

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so the letters of temper are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: p is a dictionary abbreviation for priest
taken as written

explanation.surface: We take it for granted that the vicar is bad-tempered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Assume' here means take for oneself in advance, not suppose.
explanation.definitionFit: To pre-empt is to take or seize something before others can, much as one may assume control or a right.

clue.text: Came out with rice pudding?

indicators.note: out suggests something put out of its proper order, so the letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dish arrived at the table served with rice pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rice pudding' reads as one dish; 'rice' belongs to the anagram and 'pudding' alone is the definition, the British word for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain any dessert is called pudding, and a frozen dairy treat is a common example of one.

clue.text: A sin involving acquisitiveness and rapacity, primarily

definitions.text: A sin involving acquisitiveness and rapacity, primarily

indicators.note: involving means wrapping around, so the word for sin encloses the initials
primarily means first of all, so only the opening letters are used

blocks.note: taken as written
a vice is a moral failing
the first letters of the two nouns

explanation.surface: Defining one of the deadly sins as grasping greed.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and a description of the answer: one of the seven deadly sins, defined by greed.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice is extreme greed for wealth, a traditional deadly sin made of acquisitiveness and rapacity.

clue.text: Attack plant with leg

blocks.note: in cricket the leg side of the field is also called the on side
a rush is a grasslike marsh plant

explanation.surface: An assault on a plant using one's foot.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the leg side is also called the on side, so leg can give ON.
explanation.definitionFit: An onrush is a forceful forward surge, such as a charge, so it can stand for an attack.

clue.text: Nile bend’s bad – it could comfortably make you drift off

definitions.text: it could comfortably make you drift off

indicators.note: something bad has gone wrong, so the letters are put in a corrupted order

blocks.note: taken as written; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A dangerous curve of the Nile might comfortably carry a boat off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drift off' suggests a boat on the river, but it means falling asleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Sheets and pillowcases make a bed comfortable to sleep in, helping someone doze off at night.

clue.text: Worried expression from sweetheart after prostitute turned round

indicators.note: turned round means the word for prostitute is written backwards
after puts the word for sweetheart following the other piece

blocks.note: ho is slang for a prostitute
a term of endearment for a loved one

explanation.surface: A sweetheart looks anxious after a prostitute turns to face them.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation is uttered when something goes wrong, voicing concern or dismay.

clue.text: Great bird getting excited in party – me too!

indicators.note: something excited is agitated and jumpy, so the bird's letters are shaken up
in means placed inside the word for party

blocks.note: the great tit is a common European songbird
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A guest is thrilled to see a great bird at a party and another agrees.
explanation.definitionFit: Ditto is said to show that the same applies to oneself, a way of agreeing with what someone has just said.

clue.text: I’m a metal that’s alloyed with copper to become stainless

indicators.note: alloyed metals are melted and mixed together, so these letters are blended into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A metal boasts that mixing with copper will make it stainless steel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stainless' points to steel, but it is used in its moral sense of unblemished.
explanation.definitionFit: Immaculate means spotless or free from any flaw, so it is stainless in the literal and moral sense.

clue.text: Saved European from rubbish expedition

indicators.note: saved is used in the sense of except, so the European is left out

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
tripe means nonsense or worthless stuff

explanation.surface: A European is rescued from a rubbish tip during an expedition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saved' is the old preposition meaning 'except', not rescued.
explanation.definitionFit: A trip is a journey or outing, and an expedition is an organised journey with a purpose.

clue.text: Pen with discharge at the end – problem with lid?

indicators.note: at the end points to only the final letter of the word before

blocks.note: a sty is a pen for pigs
the final letter of discharge

explanation.surface: A pen leaks ink at the tip; maybe the cap is faulty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lid' suggests the pen's cap, but here it is an eyelid; the infection does leak a discharge.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is an inflamed swelling at the edge of an eyelid, an ailment affecting the lid.

clue.text: Phoney drug taken with ecstasy ultimately makes you dance

indicators.note: ultimately means finally, so just the last letter of the word for ecstasy is used

blocks.note: hokey means fake or contrived
slang for cocaine
the final letter of ecstasy

explanation.surface: Fake drugs mixed with ecstasy at a party still get people dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: The hokey cokey is a British party dance with a sung refrain (the hokey pokey in the US). 'ecstasy' suggests E, but the last letter is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a group dance done in a circle at parties, putting limbs in and out as the song instructs.
